q.intro.text: Eight used cars of the same model: mileage and price. Three people each drew a line through them. Line A joins the first and the last car. Line B goes exactly through three cars. Line C passes through no car at all. Which line fits the data best? Pick one, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps, one line, and what its numbers mean. Press each step: the graph moves first, then the notation.

e.step0.text: Take the car with ninety-five thousand miles. Line C predicts twelve point five: twelve thousand five hundred dollars. It actually sold for fourteen thousand. The residual is observed minus predicted: fourteen minus twelve point five, which is plus one point five. Positive: the car sits above the line. It sold for fifteen hundred dollars more than predicted.

e.step1.text: Every car has a residual: one stick each. Adding them would let the pluses cancel the minuses, so square them and add. Line B hits three cars exactly, but misses the rest badly: sixty-two. Line A joins the first and the last car, and every other car sits above it: nineteen point eight. Line C: eight point six, the smallest. Line C is the least-squares line, rounded: technology finds the line with the smallest possible sum.

e.step2.text: The slope, negative zero point one two, is thousand dollars per thousand miles: for each additional thousand miles, the predicted price is a hundred and twenty dollars lower, on average. Not every car loses exactly that much. The intercept, twenty-three point nine, is the prediction at zero miles: twenty-three thousand nine hundred dollars. But zero miles is outside the data, which run from twenty to a hundred and ten thousand miles, so it only anchors the line.

e.step3.text: Technology gives r equals negative zero point nine six. Its sign is the direction: downhill. Its size, close to one, is the strength: the cars stay close to the line. Is a line the right form at all? The residual plot puts each car at its mileage and its residual. No pattern, just scatter around zero. A line is a fair model here.

e.why.text: Quick check: why does least squares square the residuals, instead of just adding them?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. Pluses and minuses cancel: a terrible line can still have residuals that add up to zero. Squares are never negative, so every miss counts.

e.why.most.text: Hitting cars exactly is not the goal. Line B went through three cars and was the worst line of all.

e.why.sum.text: Try it: a line can be far too steep and still have residuals that add to zero. A plain sum cannot tell good lines from bad ones.

t.intro.text: Your turn. Ten students: hours studied, and test score. The first steps are done for you: the pairs are in the two lists, row by row, and the linear regression ran. Its output is on the board.

t.eq.text: Which equation does the output give, with the coefficients rounded to two decimal places?

t.eq.ok.text: Yes. In y equals a plus b x, a is the intercept and b is the slope: y hat equals fifty-three point one eight, plus four point six nine x.

t.eq.swap.text: Check the form on the screen: y equals a plus b x. a, fifty-three point one eight, is the intercept. b, four point six nine, is what multiplies x.

t.eq.r.text: Zero point nine four is r, the correlation. The slope is b, four point six nine.

t.pred.text: In the data, the student who studied eight hours scored eighty-one. What does the line predict for eight hours? Give y hat to the nearest tenth.

t.pred.ok.text: Yes: fifty-three point one eight, plus four point six nine times eight, is ninety point seven points.

t.pred.swap.text: That multiplied the intercept by eight. The slope, four point six nine, is what multiplies x.

t.pred.obs.text: Eighty-one is what this student actually scored. The prediction is the height of the line at x equals eight.

t.pred.no.text: Put x equals eight into the line: fifty-three point one eight, plus four point six nine x.

t.res.text: That student scored eighty-one. What is the residual: observed minus predicted?

t.res.ok.text: Yes: eighty-one minus ninety point seven is negative nine point seven. Negative: the student is below the line.

t.res.sign.text: Observed minus predicted: eighty-one minus ninety point seven. The student is below the line, so the residual is negative.

t.res.no.text: The residual is observed minus predicted: eighty-one minus ninety point seven.

t.mean.text: What does a residual of negative nine point seven say about this student?

t.mean.ok.text: Yes: the student scored nine point seven points less than the line predicts for eight hours of study.

t.mean.under.text: Under-predicting would put the student above the line. A negative residual is below it: the model predicted too much.

t.mean.bare.text: The student scored eighty-one. The residual compares that with the prediction: nine point seven points below it.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked line C, and you were right: it has the smallest sum of squared residuals. That is the least-squares criterion.

q.cb.first.text: At the start you picked line A. Joining the first and last points ignores the rest: here, every other car sat above it.

q.cb.most.text: At the start you picked line B. Going exactly through three cars left the others far away: its sum of squares was the largest.

q.cb.none.text: The best line is the one with the smallest sum of squared residuals: the least-squares line.

p.intro.text: Riley fits a line to the stopping distance of one car on dry pavement, against its speed, and technology gives r equals zero point nine nine. Riley says: r is almost one, so a straight line is the right model for stopping distance. Is Riley right?

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. The residual plot is the test of form: a U shape means the data bend.

p.c2.text: Right. Curved data leave a straight line too low at the ends and too high in the middle. It misses in a system, not by chance.

p.c3.text: Right. r measures how closely points follow some straight line. Points on a gentle curve can still give r near one.

p.no.highR.text: That is exactly Riley's slip. A curve can give r near one: only the residual plot shows whether the form is right.

p.no.small.text: Small or not, residuals that follow a pattern mean the line is off in a system. At seventy miles per hour it is twenty feet short, and that matters when you brake.

p.no.pct.text: r is not a percent of right predictions. Almost every prediction here misses a little.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That's a proof. Riley's r is real, but it cannot show the form is right. The residual plot can, and here it says: curve.
